Chaldeans
kăl-dē'ănz
n. pl. (the people of southern Babylonia — the nation God raised to destroy Jerusalem, and, in Daniel, the caste of Babylon's wise men)
From Hebrew Kasdi or Kasdim, Chaldeans, of uncertain origin; the KJV renders the same word both “Chaldeans” and, in Gen 11:31, “Chaldees”. The Greek Chaldaios follows the Hebrew.

Biblical Definition

The Chaldeans carry two senses in Scripture and both matter. Ethnically and politically they are the people of southern Mesopotamia who came to rule Babylon, and Habakkuk records the LORD's answer to a prophet complaining about violence in Judah: “lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs” (Hab 1:6). It was an answer that appalled him — how can a holier God use a filthier nation? — and the whole of Habakkuk 2 is the reply. These are the men who burned the temple, blinded Zedekiah, and carried Judah to the rivers of Babylon. The second sense is technical: in Daniel the Chaldeans are a professional order, listed with “the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers” (Dan 2:2) — the learned caste of the empire, masters of omens and star-reading, who could not tell the king his dream. Daniel could, and the contrast is the book's argument: revelation from the God of heaven against the entire apparatus of Babylonian divination. The dynasty ends in a sentence: “In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain” (Dan 5:30). And it began, long before, with a call out of Ur of the Chaldees.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Chaldean as pertaining to Chaldea, and notes the secondary use of the name for the class of astrologers and men of learning at Babylon.

expand to see more

CHALDEAN, n. An inhabitant of Chaldea, a country of Asia lying on the lower Euphrates about Babylon.

The Chaldeans succeeded the Assyrians in the empire of the east, and under Nebuchadnezzar subdued Judea.

Also, one of an order of philosophers, astrologers and diviners at Babylon, famed for the observation of the stars.

CHALDEE, n. The language of the Chaldeans, a dialect of the Aramean, in which parts of Daniel and Ezra are written.

Ur of the Chaldees was the city from which Abram was called.

Key Scripture

Hab 1:6 — "For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs."

Dan 2:2 — "Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king."

Dan 5:30 — "In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain."

Gen 11:31 — "And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there."

Modern Corruption

Astrology is treated as harmless entertainment; Daniel treats the Chaldean art as the empire's official rival to revelation, and shows it failing in the one thing that mattered.

expand to see more

Daniel 2 is the Bible's set-piece against divination, and it is worth seeing how it is staged. The Chaldeans are not charlatans on a street corner; they are the intellectual establishment of the greatest empire on earth, salaried, credentialed, consulted by the king. And their answer to a straightforward demand is that no man can do it. Then a captive Hebrew says the thing that reframes everything: “there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets” (Dan 2:28). The horoscope column and the app that reads a birth chart are the same art with the majesty stripped out, and Scripture's objection is not that it fails to work but that it seeks from the creature what only the Creator gives. Deu 18:10-12 lists the whole apparatus and calls the practitioners an abomination.

The second thing to name is the answer Habakkuk received, because the modern instinct is to soften it. God said He was raising up a nation more wicked than the one He was judging, and He did not apologise for it. Habakkuk's protest — “wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?” (Hab 1:13) — is answered by a delay and a promise: the vision is for an appointed time, the proud shall fall, “but the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4). That verse became the hinge of the Reformation, and it was quarried out of a complaint about the Chaldeans.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kasdim (H3778), Chaldeans; Aramaic Kasday (H3779); 'ashshaph (H825), astrologer or enchanter.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kasdim (H3778) — Chaldeans, Chaldees; the nation and, in Daniel, the learned order.

Aramaic Kasday (H3779) — Chaldean; used in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.

Hebrew 'ashshaph (H825) — an astrologer, conjurer; listed beside the Chaldeans in Dan 2:2.

Hebrew chartom (H2748) — a magician, one skilled in sacred writing; the same caste in Egypt and Babylon.

Hebrew raz (H7328) — a secret, mystery; the thing Daniel says only the God of heaven reveals.

Usage

"“Lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation” — the answer that appalled a prophet."

"“The magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans” — the establishment that could not."

"“Ur of the Chaldees” — where the call of Abram began."
